introduction: “Your hands and feet will be working but your heart must be attached to the Almighty.” The guide’s first move excludes the hermit’s answer; its third reading rejects asceticism outright; and then, for a hundred sentences, it urges the reader to rise above “the world of nature”: to be more than the animal that is nature’s captive, to master nature by knowledge, to be born out of it, to fly. Paul’s “set your affection on things above”, the pilgrims of Hebrews, the Upanishad’s “from the unreal lead me to the real”, the Buddha’s middle way, Mill’s Socrates dissatisfied and Pascal’s thinking reed are all near. The opposition is a serious one, and partly scriptural: “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good”; “every creature of God is good”. Hopkins praises dappled things, Whitman will be the poet of the body as of the soul, Tagore finds freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. And Pascal warns that whoever would act the angel acts the brute.
questions: The readings call nature “darkness upon darkness”; Genesis calls creation “very good”. What do the readings mean by “the world of nature” that lets both be true?
Tagore finds deliverance “in a thousand bonds of delight”, not in renunciation. Readings 2 and 3 also reject renunciation. Where do Tagore and the readings part, if they do?
Bacon says nature is commanded by being obeyed. In what sense do humans “breach nature’s law” (10, 20), and in what sense do they never do so?
“He who would act the angel acts the brute.” Which readings in the guide show awareness of that danger?
Paul and Silas sing in prison; Lovelace says stone walls do not make one. What exactly is claimed in readings 66 to 70: that suffering is not felt, or something else?
Reading 90 praises a people without physicians, while a reported saying of the Prophet commends treatment. How should a reader weigh a single talk against the wider teaching?

outside.why: “Your hands and feet will be working but your heart must be attached to the Almighty.” Jesus prays not that his friends be taken out of the world, but that they be kept from the evil.

Tagore: deliverance is not for me in renunciation; I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. He will not shut the doors of his senses. The reading wants the hands in the world and the heart elsewhere. Are these the same position or opposed ones?

Ascetic hardship weakens the powers of nature, the reading says, and is not the way. Paul on “touch not; taste not; handle not”: such things have a shew of wisdom in neglecting of the body, and are of no value.
The Buddha’s first sermon rejects both extremes, devotion to pleasure and devotion to self-mortification, for a middle way.
The reading quotes this saying: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal.
“Man ever aspires to greater heights.” Browning: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for?

Man’s function is to redeem himself “from the inherent defects of nature”. Pope places him on this isthmus of a middle state, a being darkly wise and rudely great, in doubt to deem himself a god or beast.
The life of man is “divine, eternal, not mortal and sensual”. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.

To be satisfied with eating, drinking and sleeping is the lowest point. Mill: it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
Jesus in the wilderness, hungry, quotes Deuteronomy to the same purpose: man shall not live by bread alone.

Through knowledge humans “can breach nature’s law”. Bacon, the prophet of that power, put it more carefully: nature to be commanded must be obeyed. Is mastery over nature a breaking of its order or a deeper submission to it?
He seeks knowledge of everything except God. Thoreau on the inventions of his age: they are but improved means to an unimproved end.
Knowledge exalts and ignorance debases. Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.
The earthworm thinks intelligence is to delve downward. Plato’s Socrates says the soul, until philosophy takes it in hand, views existence through the bars of a prison and wallows in ignorance.
The higher nature is to overcome the lower. Pascal’s warning to all who try: man is neither angel nor brute, and the unfortunate thing is that he who would act the angel acts the brute.
“The world of nature is darkness upon darkness.” Genesis: God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. How can both be said of one world?

Hopkins gives glory for dappled things, skies of couple-colour, finches’ wings, all trades and their gear. His praise goes through matter, not past it. What do the readings mean by “nature” that such praise does not contradict them?
Man is saved from the grasp of nature. To be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.

The animal is nature’s captive; man discovers. Pascal: were the universe to crush him, man would still be nobler than that which kills him, because he knows that he dies; the universe knows nothing of this.
Genesis gives the charter of that discovering power in its first chapter: replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion.
Man must be “spiritually born again out and away from the womb of nature”. Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
“God created them free.” Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.

Freedom is deliverance from captivity to nature. Rousseau, of all people, agrees on the definition: the mere impulse of appetite is slavery, while obedience to a law we prescribe to ourselves is liberty.
Paradise and the Fire are two states of one’s own gaze. Milton gives the thought to Satan, who misuses it: the mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven.
No service without freedom from desire. What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
The pure heart, like a mirror, reflects the sun from any distance. Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
The love of God is the bond not subject to corruption. The world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
These souls “speak of another world and call to another realm”. Paul: our conversation is in heaven.
How long will human birds nest in this dust-heap? Here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
The eagle soaring to the heights. They shall mount up with wings as eagles.
“Spread thy wings and fly.” Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest.
Yeats, old, sails for a city of the spirit: an aged man is but a paltry thing, unless soul clap its hands and sing; once out of nature I shall never take my bodily form from any natural thing.
“Pass beyond the world and set your face toward the city of the Beloved.” They confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth; they desire a better country.
“Be thou oblivious of this world below.” Whitman: I am the poet of the Body and I am the poet of the Soul. He refuses to rank them. What would be lost, on his account, by obliviousness?

The pastoral letter, against those who forbade marriage and meats: every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. How does the first reading of the guide, with its working hands, guard this one?
On earth, and yet in heaven. Though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.
Pass beyond this plane to behold the lights of the realm above. The Upanishad’s prayer: lead me from the unreal to the real, lead me from darkness to light, lead me from death to immortality.
For sovereignty over both worlds, set your foot on the crown of this one. Jesus is offered all the kingdoms of the world, and refuses them.
The lights of earthly sovereignty fade. Round the decay of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretch far away.
“The physical world has no authority.” Epictetus: men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
His soul soars though his body lie at the bottom of a pit. Stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
“God hath changed the prison into the Most Exalted Horizon.” At midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God.
Then pain is as pleasure. Troubled on every side, yet not distressed; perplexed, but not in despair; cast down, but not destroyed.
Men are killed for “dirt”, and do not know why. Wilfred Owen, from the trenches: what passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
Fix not your gaze on these fleeting days. We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal.
If the earthen house was burned, build your nest elsewhere. If our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God.
Those whose lives were limited to material concerns have left no trace. Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be?
When people meet, the talk is all of acquiring wealth. Wordsworth: the world is too much with us; late and soon, getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
A man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Spiritual health matters more than bodily. Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.

A people is described who have no doctors and submit to God. The Prophet is reported to have said that God has sent down no disease without also sending down its treatment. Elsewhere the Bahá’í writings command recourse to physicians. How is this reading’s praise of simplicity to be read with them?
“No man can be happy without God, though he may not know why he is miserable.” Our hearts are restless till they rest in Thee.
A prayer that happiness be “divine in origin and not parasitical”. Thoreau’s diagnosis of the other kind: the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
Freedom comes by attaching no importance to material things. Emerson: things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.
God “has made us masters over the material world. Shall we then become her slaves?” Thou madest him to have dominion over the works of thy hands; thou hast put all things under his feet.

shortfall: Many of the readings are brief exhortations in a single image (spread thy wings; pass beyond this world; be free of nature) addressed to individuals; a companion was given to each image and argument, not to each letter.
